web_text_verbatim: Fracture of the 5th (and sometimes 4th) metacarpal neck resulting from direct impact with a clenched fist.
focus: Boxer's fracture - 5th metacarpal neck mechanism and pattern
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: Lastly, boxing or trauma induced with a closed fist results in a high frequency of metacarpal neck fractures. The most common metacarpal fracture occurs in the fifth metacarpal neck, which has been referred to as a “boxer’s fracture.”

web_text_verbatim: Intra-articular 2-part fracture-subluxation of the base of the 1st metacarpal pulled proximally and radially by the APL tendon
focus: Bennett fracture - volar ulnar fragment with proximal-radial shaft subluxation
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: The Bennett fracture is a volar ulnar intra-articular fracture fragment of the metacarpal base with resultant subluxation of the remaining metacarpal shaft, which displaces proximally, radially, and dorsally.

web_text_verbatim: Comminuted T- or Y-shaped intra-articular fracture at the base of the 1st metacarpal
focus: Rolando fracture - high energy comminuted T/Y-shaped intra-articular pattern
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: Rolando fractures are similar to Bennett fractures but often result from a higher amount of energy imparted on the joint resulting in a Y- or T-shaped fracture pattern with more significant intra-articular extension.

web_text_verbatim: Extra-articular distal radius fracture within 2-3 cm of the articular surface with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation (dinner-fork deformity)
focus: Colles fracture - dorsally angulated, apex volar extra-articular distal radius fracture
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: The most commonly used eponym is that of Colles, who first described the pattern of a dorsally angulated, apex volar metaphyseal distal radius fracture in 1814. It is meant to refer to extra-articular fractures

web_text_verbatim: Distal radius fracture with volar (palmar) displacement and volar angulation of distal fragment (garden spade deformity, reverse Colles)
focus: Smith fracture - volarly angulated, apex dorsal metaphyseal fracture
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: It is the opposite of the Smith fracture, which described a volarly angulated, apex dorsal metaphyseal distal radius fracture.

web_text_verbatim: Fracture-dislocation of the radiocarpal joint involving the intra-articular volar (volar Barton) or dorsal (dorsal Barton) rim of the distal radius with carpal subluxation
focus: Barton fracture - intra-articular rim fracture with radiocarpal subluxation/dislocation
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: The Barton fracture refers to an intra-articular distal radius fracture extending through the dorsal cortex of the radius, often with dorsal subluxation or dislocation of the radiocarpal joint. A volar or reverse Barton describes a fracture that extends out the volar aspect of the distal radius and there may be subluxation or dislocation in that direction.

web_text_verbatim: Intra-articular avulsion fracture of the radial styloid process from direct scaphoid impaction (Hutchinson fracture)
focus: Chauffeur's fracture - isolated intra-articular radial styloid fracture
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: A Chauffeur’s fracture is an isolated intra-articular fracture of the radial styloid, so named because it was caused by the engine backfiring while chauffeurs were starting the earliest generation of automobiles with a hand crank on the front.

web_text_verbatim: Fracture of the distal third of the radial shaft with disruption and dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ); fracture of necessity
focus: Galeazzi fracture - fracture of necessity (radius shaft + DRUJ dislocation)
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Campbell 14th ed.
quote: fracture of the distal or middle third of the shaf of the radius and dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint was called “the fracture of necessity” by Campbell.

web_text_verbatim: Spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft with high propensity for entrapment or laceration of the radial nerve
focus: Holstein-Lewis fracture - distal spiral humeral fracture with radial nerve entrapment risk
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: In 1963, Holstein and Lewis associated a special type of fracture of the distal humerus, a simple displaced spiral fracture, with the distal end deviating toward the radial side occurring in about 7% of all humeral shaft fractures, with an increased rate of radial nerve palsy (Fig. 37-4).131 They reported a high incidence of entrapment of the nerve within this type of fracture and recommended radial nerve exploration in the presence of clinical symptoms.

web_text_verbatim: Fracture of the femoral head occurring in conjunction with traumatic posterior dislocation of the hip joint
focus: Pipkin fracture - femoral head fracture with posterior hip dislocation
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: Epstein’s type V dislocation includes a femoral head fracture. This type has been subdivided by Pipkin into four types (Fig. 52-8).99 This scheme is commonly used and is important in decision making.

web_text_verbatim: Avulsion fracture of the lateral tibial plateau at the insertion of the Anterolateral Ligament (ALL); highly associated with ACL tear
focus: Segond fracture - lateral tibial plateau avulsion / ALL injury
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: Another bony avulsion injury may be associated with the anterolateral ligament (ALL). These fractures are commonly referred to as Segond fractures and represent an injury to the anterolateral (AL) capsule of the knee.

web_text_verbatim: Fracture of the talar neck caused by hyperdorsiflexion of the foot against the floorboard or rudder bar in a plane crash.
focus: Aviator's astragalus - talar neck fracture from dorsiflexion impact on rudder bar
suggested_fix: None needed. Confirmed in Rockwood 10th ed.
quote: In 1919, Anderson reported on a series of 18 fracture-dislocations of the talus in pilots of the Royal Flying Corps.3 It was the first descriptions on the mechanism of injury: dorsiflexion at the ankle with axial force, as a result of the rudder bar hitting the foot on impact in a crash landing. He called this injury “aviator’s astragalus.”
